content: Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV is a devastating outcome of the HIV epidemic, particularly in resource-limited settings. Each year, approximately 650,000 new pediatric HIV infections occur globally due to MTCT. This pediatric HIV epidemic poses a significant threat to longstanding child survival programs. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of vaginal disinfection on the risk of MTCT of HIV, as well as its effects on infant and maternal mortality and morbidity. Additionally, the study aimed to assess the tolerability of vaginal disinfection in HIV-infected pregnant women. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Register, PubMed, EMBASE, AIDSLINE, LILACS, AIDSTRIALS, and AIDSDRUGS. Standardized methodological filters were used to identify trials. Further sources included reference lists of identified articles, editorials, expert opinions, letters to journal editors, conference abstracts, and proceedings. Experts in the field and pharmaceutical companies were also contacted. No language restrictions were applied during the search. The inclusion criteria for the study required randomized or clinical trials that compared vaginal disinfection during labor with either placebo or no treatment in HIV-infected pregnant women. These trials needed to provide data on the effect of vaginal disinfection on MTCT of HIV, as well as on infant and maternal mortality and morbidity. Three authors independently evaluated the eligibility and quality of the trials and extracted the relevant data. A meta-analysis was performed using the Yusuf-Peto modification of Mantel-Haenszel's fixed-effect method. Only two trials, involving a total of 708 participants, met the inclusion criteria. The findings indicated that the effect of vaginal disinfection on the risk of MTCT of HIV was uncertain, with an odds ratio (OR) of 0.93 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.65 to 1.33). Similarly, the effect on neonatal death (OR 1.38, 95% CI 0.30 to 6.33) and death after the neonatal period (OR 1.45, 95% CI 0.47 to 4.45) was also uncertain. There was no evidence to suggest that vaginal disinfection increased adverse effects in mothers (OR 1.15, 95% CI 0.41 to 3.22). However, evidence from one trial indicated a reduction in adverse effects in neonates (OR 0.14, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.31). In conclusion, there is currently no evidence to support the effectiveness of vaginal disinfection in reducing the risk of MTCT of HIV. Given the simplicity and low cost of this intervention, there is a pressing need for a large, well-designed, and rigorously conducted randomized controlled trial to evaluate the potential additive effect of vaginal disinfection on MTCT of HIV in women receiving antiretroviral therapy.
